name: Taiga folk
one_line: They followed the reindeer through the snow forest and lived on birch: bark for the boat and the box, fungus off the trunk to carry the fire, pitch out of the old pine stumps.

needs: a stand of birch among the conifers
a stream, or a lake beyond the lake folk's 200 m, for fish
lichen ground within a day's walk for the herd's winter

staples: fish from the lakes and rivers (whitefish, pike, trout)
berries: bilberry, lingonberry, cloudberry off the bog
pine inner bark, dried and ground
moose, hare and grouse in season
how: net and spear in the lake; a line through the ice
the herd: followed in summer, penned and milked in autumn
snares on the hare runs; berries by the basketful
bark peeled from the pines in spring when the sap rises
preserve: the winter itself: meat frozen in the store
cloudberries keep in their own juice, lingonberries in water
a store on a post the animals cannot climb

fuel.note: spruce and pine logs for the long night; dead branch snapped off the lower trunk; birch logs where the stand allows; birch bark and fatwood splints are kindling, never the fire

shelter.form: a pole tent whose cover travels with the herd and whose frame is left standing; a turf hut over a skin of birch bark for winter; a store on one post; racks between the trees

TAIGA.fuel: spruce and pine logs, birch where it grows; fatwood out of the old stumps
TAIGA.food: lake fish on the rack, bilberry and lingonberry underfoot, the herd in the lichen woods all winter
TAIGA.shelter: turf-and-bark hut under the spruce, a bark tent in summer, a store on a post
TAIGA.palette: spruce black-green, birch white, lichen grey, ember red

KRUMMHOLZ.fuel: scarce: wind-killed branch off the flagged spruce, dwarf birch and willow bundles; bark and fatwood carried up from the forest
KRUMMHOLZ.food: the herd's summer edge: milk at the pens, cloudberry and heath berry, char from the tarns
KRUMMHOLZ.shelter: a hide tent turned from the wind and pitched behind a rock; no hut, nobody winters here
KRUMMHOLZ.palette: flagged spruce, larch gold, lichen white, bare grey stone

knows: bilberry, lingonberry, cloudberry: which bog, which month
pine inner bark: spring only, one side of the tree
tinder fungus and chaga on the birch trunks
Labrador tea: a few leaves, never a strong brew
reindeer lichen: the herd's winter, decades to regrow
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why the birch matters more than the spruce; which stump smells of pitch when it is split; why the old camps grow fireweed and nettle
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: cloudberry against scurvy through the dark months; peel bark on one side and the pine lives to be peeled again; the hoof-shaped fungus holds a coal, the black one makes tea

makes: a canoe hull sewn with root and sealed with pitch
wants_from_player: a clay pot (the pitch is cooked in it)

techniques.name: Ember carrier
techniques.verb: take a live coal from the hearth, bed it in tinder fungus and punk wood, fold birch bark around it
techniques.teaches: fire is never made, only carried: a people who move with a herd take the hearth with them in a fungus the size of a fist. It gives no light, it goes cold if you forget it, and every fire it lays is the old fire moved
techniques.unlocks: carry fire for a day or more with no light; lay a new fire from it; it goes cold if neglected

techniques.name: Birch bark
techniques.verb: peel the outer bark in sheets in early summer when it lifts; sew boxes with split root; take the tinder fungus off the same trunk
techniques.teaches: the birch is the taiga's clay: it holds water, sheds rain, burns wet, and the tree lives on if you take only the outer skin
techniques.unlocks: containers, a canoe, the ember carrier's wrap; the bark-worker's craft

techniques.name: Resin torch
techniques.verb: twist a strip of bark, dip it in pine pitch
techniques.teaches: a torch that shrugs off drizzle and burns brighter and longer; pitch is what the forest gives instead of fat
techniques.unlocks: a torch that burns longer and brighter and shrugs off drizzle (torch.json resin block)

techniques.name: Fatwood
techniques.verb: split the resin-soaked heart out of an old pine stump; it is dark, heavy and smells of turpentine
techniques.teaches: a hot, long torch found not made: the stump hardened after the tree died, and the older the stump the better the wood
techniques.unlocks: fatwood splints: a hot, long-burning torch that lights wet; kindling that catches from a coal

techniques.name: Drying and smoking
techniques.verb: racks between two spruces in the wind, or over a slow smoky fire in the hut
techniques.teaches: the first storage: fish and meat keep through the dark months
techniques.unlocks: fish and meat keep through the lean season

techniques.name: Pitch and tar
techniques.verb: cook pine resin in a pot; or pack resinous wood and birch bark in a turf-covered pit and burn it slow until the tar runs out the bottom
techniques.teaches: the same fire that cooks food can cook a tree into glue; one pit seals a boat and a hundred torches
techniques.unlocks: glue for the spear, tar for the canoe seams and the torches; the camp's trade good downriver

techniques.name: The herd
techniques.verb: follow the reindeer, then keep them: pen and milk them in autumn, walk them to the lichen woods for winter and up to the treeline for summer
techniques.teaches: the taiga's fundamental: food, hide and a beast to carry the tent where nothing can be planted; built last
techniques.unlocks: the taiga's food ceiling; milk, hide, antler and sinew; the fence and the pen

ladder: fire in the lee of the spruce
fish from the lake, berries from the bog
racks and the store on a post
the bark-worker: boxes, the canoe, tar
tar and bark go downriver; salt comes back
growth.restraint: bark is peeled from one side of a living pine and some cambium always left, so the tree lives and is peeled again in a generation; the herd is moved before the lichen is grazed out (it regrows in decades, not seasons); tar wood comes from old stumps and standing dead, not the living stand
growth.ceiling_hint: the herd is built last in the engine, so until it exists fish and forage carry a taiga camp to a handful; with the herd (lichen woods for winter, a treeline edge for summer) it reaches the tribal ceiling; a krummholz site alone is a summer camp that never grows

signatures.what: a ring of fire-cracked stones under the moss, often several in a row where the tents stood; the ground around them greener
signatures.restore: cleared: the new camp's fire goes on the old stones
signatures.inherits: a dry floor, and ground that grows nettle and fireweed

signatures.what: a living pine with a long scar face on one side, bark healed in over the edges; a loose line of them along the old trail. Readable from the first: nothing to restore
signatures.restore: restored: the plantkeeper peels the far side; the scar says the tree was fed on before
signatures.inherits: bark flour from the first spring, and proof the site fed people for centuries

signatures.what: a funnel-shaped hollow with a black, hard bottom and a channel out the low side; nothing grows in it
signatures.restore: restored: cleared of needles and relined with turf

signatures.what: a line of post stubs gone to moss, closing on a stone pen; grass where the herd stood
signatures.restore: restored: new poles on the old stubs
signatures.inherits: the pen works from the first autumn; the herd ceiling opens early

signatures.what: four post stumps in a square, or one thick one, where the store stood clear of the animals
signatures.restore: restored: a new store on the old post

ruin.plants_differ: nettle and fireweed in a ring on the old hearths (bone, ash and dung), grass in the pen where the forest floor is otherwise moss and lichen; and the bark-stripped pines, scarred on the side that faced the trail

aesthetic.silhouette: a pole tent among black spruce; a store on one post; racks like ladders between trunks; white birch against the dark
sounds: the crack of a birch log

real_world.region: Sápmi: northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola Peninsula; a living people
real_world.note: reindeer herding grew out of wild-reindeer hunting; rows of stone hearths at inland sites dated 1000–1300 AD mark the change. The lavvu (pole tent) and the goahti (a turf hut laid over birch bark on a timber frame); the njalla, a store on one smoothed post animals cannot climb. Scots pine inner bark peeled in spring, eaten fresh, roasted, or dried and ground into flour mixed with reindeer milk; scars dendro-dated to at least 1450 AD, with evidence back to c. 2800 BP; some cambium was always left so the tree lived, and the scars stand for centuries

real_world.region: Siberian taiga from the Ob to the Sea of Okhotsk; a living people
real_world.note: reindeer ridden and milked, not eaten (wild reindeer and elk were hunted); a saddle set on the shoulders; a family kept some 25 animals. Conical tents of birch bark or reindeer skin on birch poles; the frames were left standing and only the covers carried on

pines debarked years ahead so resin flooded the wood; the wood stacked in a funnel-shaped pit, covered with moss, peat and soil, and burned slow with little air for days; tar ran out the bottom after about a day. Big pits took up to 1,000 m³ of wood; exports peaked in 1863 at nearly 30 million litres

real_world.analogue: Tinder fungus and Ötzi's fire kit
real_world.region: Europe; Alps c. 3300 BCE, Star Carr (Mesolithic Britain)
real_world.note: Fomes fomentarius grows on birch in the north; its inner layer, soaked, beaten and stretched, is amadou, which catches a spark and smoulders for hours. Ötzi carried four pieces of it. Star Carr shows it in use with flint and pyrite. We keep the fungus and drop the pyrite: in our world a coal is carried in it, never struck

real_world.region: Nitassinan, the Labrador Peninsula; a living people
real_world.note: caribou provided practically all the necessities of life; a few families wintered together at hunting camps and gathered in summer. Birchbark wigwams in the south, caribou hide in the north; canoes in summer, snowshoes and toboggans in winter. Bark canoes were sewn with split spruce root and the seams sealed with hot spruce or pine resin
birch bark heated without air gives a black tar; tar-hafted tools from Königsaue and Campitello are about 200,000 years old, a Zandmotor flake about 50,000. Pitch predates the pot
